        - reason: scc matches reference (release-4.21)
      Note Some SCC creation is driven by programs, while this check is based on using reference YAML-files. So a 100% match is not always ensured. Furthermore for unset attributes with default values those get injected during the creation, while the attributes having default values and the values might change per cluster version. As a result the content of a SCC can depend on the sequence of events, eventually. Therefore it gets checked, if all updates happened during the course of a cluster update. But also this is imprecise as the update is set to complete before all minor tasks are finally completed. So please take any diff as an indication to follow-up and to leverage your subject matter experience.

    • Check 2.2.2 Master AV Zone Labels

      Context: Control plane spread across failure domains using node topology labels and hints.,Logic: Skips on Single Node OpenShift and on HyperShift clusters with external control plane (no master node data). Otherwise walks control plane nodes using `topology.kubernetes.io/region` and `topology.kubernetes.io/zone`, flags potential limitations when zones repeat, zone labels are missing (IP subnet heuristic), or subnets suggest the same AV zone; passes when successive masters land in new zones.,Goal: Highlight configurations where the gather cannot prove multi-zone control plane placement—without claiming the cluster is unsupported.
      Status WARNING

      CAUTION: At least one potential-limitation row was raised—for example duplicate zone, missing zone label with IP-based heuristic, or subnet pattern suggesting the same availability zone as another master. This does not prove the cluster is single-AZ; it only means the automation could not prove multi-AZ spread from labels and heuristics.,NOTE: Even if the test has not passed, this does not prove that the availability is limited. It just says that we cannot prove based on the data the availability. So the cluster might still meet the customer's expectation, as this is a config check only.

      Context: Cluster network sizing versus current node count.,Logic: Prints current `clusterNetwork`, `clusterNetworkMTU`, `networkType`, and `serviceNetwork` from the Network object; derives maximum node count from each `clusterNetwork` CIDR and `hostPrefix` (IPv4 formula or ipcalc-style messaging for IPv6). For non-SNO, compares current node count to that maximum: pass when headroom exists, limitation-style messaging when within 10 nodes of max, warning when count equals the theoretical maximum. SNO always gets a pass on the scalability row.,Goal: Warn before the cluster hits the addressable-node ceiling implied by SDN configuration.

      Node count is below the SDN-derived maximum with comfortable headroom (or the cluster is Single Node OpenShift where the scalability row is documented as passing by policy in the rule output).

  • Check 3.3 Custom Resource Definitions

    Context: Kubernetes Custom Resource Definitions inventory and management.,Logic: Shows the installed Kubernetes Custom Resource Definitions (CRD) in the cluster.,Goal: Document all CRDs to identify which are Red Hat-managed versus customer-managed, and monitor CRD count for API performance impact.
    Status WARNING

    CAUTION: The cluster contains some custom CRDs. It is up to the customer to maintain this list. So to ensure that no more needed CRDs get removed to avoid pollution of the system. Please mind that a growing number of CRDs has an impact on OCP-API performance which can escalate to timeouts, see KCS:"Throttling request took ... reported when running _oc get -A pod_ on OpenShift Container Platform 4" (https://access.redhat.com/solutions/5587221). The OpenShift limits are documented at: https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.21/html/scalability_and_performance/planning-your-environment-according-to-object-maximums
    Mind For all CRDs shipped with Red Hat products, Red Hat will care about the life-cycle. For all others (3rd party or homebrew) the cluster admins are responsible to manage them.
    Result

    • Check 3.5.3 ETCD Health

      Context: Comprehensive etcd health assessment.,Logic: Validates etcd health by checking the reported health status, analyzing various performance metrics, and reviewing related alerts.,Goal: Ensure etcd is healthy and performing adequately, as etcd issues can have cascading effects on the entire OpenShift cluster.
      Status PASS
      Tags has_pg_mg upgrade
      Note Kubernetes implements an event-driven architecture, whereby all Kubernetes objects and any state is backed by etcd. Therefore a correctly configured and healthy etcd is utmost essential for any OpenShift cluster. That’s why we have a special focus on etcd in the context of this review
      Result
      • etcd health check: [PASS]
        - reason: all etcd members reported to be healthy
      Important The monitoring data for etcd disk performance provides a good view on potential etcd limits and this instance seems to get close to the limits. Please note, that in this state you might still not experience any obvious degradation in your OpenShift cluster during normal operations. But as this check has not passed, please consider this a limitation for a further growth of the cluster, as the etcd might not be able to deal with the resulting additional load. Furthermore you need to expect that the etcd will more likely get into trouble when the cluster is not in "normal" operations, like during a failover or even an update roll-out. While an unhealthy etcd can have various cascading effects on the overall OCP cluster. Please monitor the etcd closely and take any etcd related alert very seriously.

    • Check 3.5.5 ETCD Compaction

      Context: etcd storage maintenance and error detection.,Logic: Analyzes etcd logs to report on storage compaction durations, various errors, and performed storage defragmentations.,Goal: Ensure etcd compaction operations complete within acceptable timeframes and identify errors that could impact etcd performance or stability.
      Status FAIL

      IMPORTANT : The etcd logs contain a worrying amount/kinds of errors. This calls for a deep manual investigation and is a very concerning sign for the etcd health! Please check etcd logs to start an investigation. If you need Red Hat assistance to resolve the underlying issues, please open a separate support case via the RH customer portal (https://access.redhat.com/support/cases/) per issue.
      Tags default_mg_only upgrade
      Result
      • etcd member etcd-ocp-control1.one.ocp4.example.com: [FAIL]
        - reason: found 95% quantile: 816ms, with 715ms as best time and 816ms as worst time
      • etcd member etcd-ocp-control2.one.ocp4.example.com: [FAIL]
        - reason: found 95% quantile: 960ms, with 756ms as best time and 960ms as worst time
      • etcd member etcd-ocp-control3.one.ocp4.example.com: [FAIL]
        - reason: found 95% quantile: 963ms, with 707ms as best time and 963ms as worst time
      NOTE: Compaction should be ideally around 200ms on smaller cluster but no more than 800-900ms on large clusters (20+ workers) and anything above could mean performance issues, see https://access.redhat.com/articles/6271341.
      Note Since etcd keeps an exact history of its keyspace, this history get periodically compacted to avoid performance degradation and eventual storage space exhaustion. The service degradation due to the compaction should be ideally below 100ms. Here the times found are worrying, as a too long service degradation can lead to severe cascading effects in the OpenShift cluster. The expected mitigation is to provide faster storage to back etcd.
      Note While the goal of compaction times below 100ms might not be generally achievable, pikes leading to durations of multiple seconds should be avoided. The goal should be to stay below 100ms for a 95% quantile for this size of cluster. What causes the spikes need to be analyzed in the underlying IO infrastructure. An approach for starting the analysis might be following How to graph etcd metrics using Prometheus to gauge Etcd performance in OpenShift. (https://access.redhat.com/solutions/5489721)
      Note The etcd compaction duration should be ideally below 100ms (and below 10ms on fast SSD/NVMe), while for a cluster of this size up to 200ms is still acceptable.

  • Check 3.13 Webhooks

    Context: Admission webhook configuration and impact on cluster operations.,Logic: Presents the webhooks currently active in the cluster and their configuration.,Goal: Create awareness of webhooks that might impact cluster operations or troubleshooting.
    Status FAIL
    Tags default_mg_only
    Note Mind it is likely driven by the functional need to touch a critical API or to have a Failure Policy other than "ignore". So even if some webhooks trigger a warning or fail, no mitigating actions are expected as this is for information only. This is reported here to inform, hoping that the admin remembers that a webhook with a specific behaviour might contribute to a situation during troubleshooting.
    Note Webhooks mostly get automatically installed in the context of products/operators. Therefore OCP-admins have no other choice than accepting these webhooks. The intention of this check here is to create awareness on the existence of these webhooks to potentially ease troubleshooting when needed.
    Result
    When an API extension webhook monitors the critical OCP API resources or its `Failure Policy` is not **Ignore**, it can have negative impact on the cluster.
    Found the following MutatingWebhookConfigurations can have negative impact on the cluster: Name Performance APIs Security APIs System APIs Virtual APIs Failure Policy agentclusterinstallmutators.admission.agentinstall.openshift.io False False False False Fail hypershift.openshift.io False False False False Fail
    Found the following ValidatingWebhookConfigurations can have negative impact on the cluster: Name Performance APIs Security APIs System APIs Virtual APIs Failure Policy multicluster-observability-operator False False False False Fail
    To retrieve the complete list of **MutatingWebhookConfiguration** objects, use the following command: ``` $ echo -e "Name Performance APIs Security APIs System APIs Virtual APIs Failure Policy" && oc get MutatingWebhookConfiguration -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{" false false false false "}{.webhooks[*].failurePolicy}{" "}{end}' ```
    To retrieve the complete list of **ValidatingWebhookConfiguration** objects, use the following command: ``` $ echo -e "Name Performance APIs Security APIs System APIs Virtual APIs Failure Policy" && oc get ValidatingWebhookConfiguration -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{" false false false false "}{.webhooks[*].failurePolicy}{" "}{end}' ```
    Critical OCP API resources: - Performance APIs : The webhook monitors APIs in namespaces with label `openshift.io/run-level="0"` that are likely to become performance bottlenecks. - Security APIs : The webhook monitors APIs that expose sensitive data. - System APIs : The webhook monitors system APIs (e.g. CRDs). Such webhooks are prone to cause system deadlock conditions and other system availability issues. - Virtual APIs : The webhook monitors virtual APIs (e.g. `authorization.openshift.io/v1/SelfSubjectRulesReview`). Applying a policy engine to virtual APIs is unusual.
    Get more information from https://github.com/openshift/enhancements/blob/master/enhancements/kube-apiserver/api-webhook-supportability.md
    Warning When an API extension webhook monitors the critical OCP API resources or its Failure Policy is not Ignore, it can have a negative impact on the cluster.
    Note Critical OCP API resources:
    • Performance APIs: The webhook monitors APIs in namespaces with label `openshift.io/run-level="0"` that are likely to become performance bottlenecks.
    • Security APIs : The webhook monitors APIs that expose sensitive data.
    • System APIs: The webhook monitors system APIs (e.g. CRDs). Such webhooks are prone to cause system deadlock conditions and other system availability issues.
    • Virtual APIs: The webhook monitors virtual APIs (e.g. `authorization.openshift.io/v1/SelfSubjectRulesReview`). Applying a policy engine to virtual APIs is unusual.
    Get more information from https://github.com/openshift/enhancements/blob/master/enhancements/kube-apiserver/api-webhook-supportability.md

    • Check 3.14.1 Platform Load Balancer

      Context: Load balancer configuration for API and ingress traffic.,Logic: Reports if an external load balancer is in use or an OpenShift managed appliance.,Goal: Document load balancer configuration and ensure proper health check configuration.
      Status INFO
      Result
      • loadbalancer management check: [INFO]
        - IPI installer, on platform "baremetal", so OpenShift created and manages a keepalived instance used manage inbound traffic.
      Note The API load balancer must be configured to take a maximum of 30 seconds from the time the API server turns off the /readyz endpoint to the removal of the API server instance from the pool. Within the time frame after /readyz returns an error or becomes healthy, the endpoint must have been removed or added. Probing every 5 or 10 seconds, with two successful requests to become healthy and three to become unhealthy, are well-tested values.

      Note Some SCC creation is driven by programs, while this check is based on using reference YAML-files. So a 100% match is not always ensured. Furthermore for unset attributes with default values those get injected during the creation, while the attributes having default values and the values might change per cluster version. As a result the content of a SCC can depend on the sequence of events, eventually. Therefore it gets checked, if all updates happened before the latest operator update, which is expected to have triggered a reconciliation. But also this is unprecise, eventually. So please take any diff as an indication to follow-up and to leverage your subject matter experience.

  • Check 5.1 Node Kubelet Health

    Validate if the Kublet on all nodes reports to be healthy
    Status WARNING

    At least one node shows an unexplained KubeletReady transition or a MemoryPressure / DiskPressure / PIDPressure pattern that suggests recent overload or manual recovery—investigate kubelet health, capacity, and node logs before the issue escalates.
    Tags odf
    Note On a perfectly healthy node the Kublet is expected to restart triggered by an update of the node or a roll-out of machine configuration only. Therefore it gets checked here if the reported "ready since" timestamp is related to one of those activities. If not, it can be assumed that either the node was unhealthy or an admin took manual action.
    Note Furthermore a differences in the timestamps between "KubletReady" and "DiskPressure", "MemoryPressure" or "PIDPressure" is an indication that the node was overloaded and had to take massive action (kill pods) to recover from this situation.

    • Check 6.1.2 Requests and Limits

      Present container resource configurations to support a review of those
      Status WARNING
      Tags has_pg_mg managed
      Note When the resource request gets specified for containers in a Pod, the kube-scheduler uses this information to decide which node to place the Pod on. When you specify a resource limit for a container, the kubelet enforces those limits so that the running container is not allowed to use more of that resource than the limit you set. The kubelet also reserves at least the requested amount of that system resource specifically for that container to use. More details get be found at Requests and limits (https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers/#requests-and-limits).
      While in the section Quota and Limits we took a look if the specification or resources is done and enforced, we check the settings here.
      Result
      • deploymentconfig container resources check: [NOT APPLICABLE]
        - reason: no deploymentconfig found
      • [INFO]
        DEPLOYMENTS
      • [INFO]
        | Result | Namespace | Pod | Container | CPU Lim | CPU Req | CPU Msg | Mem Lim | Mem Req | Mem Msg | QoS Class |
      • [INFO]
        | ----------- | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------ | ------- | ------- | ------- | ------- | ------- | ------- | ----------- |
      • Result messages related to CPU
      • [LIMITATION]
        (1) Container is limited by nodes resources only, what can lead to cpu throttling - while planed to not consume any.
      • [LIMITATION]
        (3) Container is limited by nodes resources only, while a consumption is planed.
      • [LIMITATION]
        (4) CPU limits significant larger than requested, what can lead to cpu throttling
      • [PASS]
        (2) Container has cpu limit, which get copied and uses as the requested value.
      • [PASS]
        (5) CPU limits larger than requested, but on an reasonable level
      • [PASS]
        (6) CPU limits is equal requested
      • Result messages related to Memory
      • [WARNING]
        (A) Container is limited by nodes resources only, while planed to not consume any.
      • [WARNING]
        (C) Container is limited by nodes resources only, while a consumption is planed.
      • [WARNING]
        (D) Memory limits significant larger than requested can lead to node memory pressure
      • [PASS]
        (B) Container has memory limit, which get copied and uses as the requested value.
      • [PASS]
        (E) Memory limits larger than requested, but on an reasonable level
      • [PASS]
        (F) Memory limits is equal requested
      Note Allowing some overcommitment on cpu is a common practice. This is based on the assumption that not all workloads will have their cpu spike at the same point in time. So that on average across all processes the cpu will not be overloaded. Even if the cpu gets overloaded, the expected impact is that response times increase. In a certain range and for a very limited duration a LINUX based system can stand that, so can Kubernetes and therefore also OpenShift.
      For some technologies, like Java, it is even needful to set the cpu limits significantly higher than requests, as just during the startup the JVM needs much more cpu to do the JIT compile, than during normal application execution.
      As memory is not compressible and swap is disabled for good reasons, any overcommitment on memory needs to be avoided. As soon as the kubelet experiences MemoryPressure it will try to evict pods. If the eviction is not fast enough the situation escalates and the kubelet reports the node and itself as unhealthy. The consequence is a restart of the kubelet including a forced eviction of all pods. The eviction of any pod will create an event the kube-scheduler will react to to reschedule the pod. If multiple nodes are close to experiencing MemoryPressure, this rescheduling can lead to cascading effects across the cluster.
      Please also mind in this context that while if a cpu spike of an application is over it will instantly no longer consume that much cpu. While most technologies will keep requested system memory for some time - some might even never decrease from what they max requested once. So nodes can hardly recover from giving more memory to a pod than planned.

Node pruning would be a relief here, but not even half of that amount is marked as reclaimable. So this might not be sufficient to avoid the node's disk pressure. To free node resources using garbage collection, please check https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.21/html/nodes/nodes/nodes-nodes-garbage-collection.html.
        Links

    • Check 6.1.6 Infra Node Workloads

      Context: Workload segregation and infrastructure node compliance.,Logic: Checks if the current workloads on infra-nodes meet the criteria for those.,Goal: Ensure infrastructure nodes only run permitted workloads according to subscription guidelines and technical requirements.
      Status NA
      Tags has_pg_mg
      Note The concept of infra-nodes has both a technical and a commercial aspect. For the purpose of a Technical Supportability Review we focus on the technical aspect. This means that we are looking to see that the workload segregation works as expected. This is primarily done by checking the configuration, and subsequently validating the pods currently running on these nodes.
      Validating the currently running pods introduces the commercial aspect. The 'Subscription Requirements for OpenShift Node Types and Features' section of the OpenShift Sizing Guide (https://www.redhat.com/en/resources/self-managed-openshift-subscription-guide#section-4) defines permitted workloads. This wording may change or leave some room for interpretation. In addition, the list of included products is under active development, so the pods encountered may change over time. Therefore this result can be misleading, as it might contain false positives. Importantly, this is a commercial aspect which the Technical Supportability Review is not entitled, nor intending, to rule on.
      Result

        - reason: no nodes with node-role label "infra"
      Note To qualify as an infrastructure node and use the included entitlement, only components that are supporting the cluster, and not part of an end-user application, may be running on those instances.
      Note Take marked workloads as a trigger to check and adjust, if required. More info on chapter 'Infrastructure nodes' in https://www.redhat.com/en/resources/self-managed-openshift-sizing-subscription-guide

      Validate the pod liveness configuration against the collected metrics
      Status SKIP WITH CONTENT
      Tags has_pg_mg managed
      Note A liveness probe determines if a container is still running. If the liveness probe fails due to a condition such as a deadlock, the kubelet kills the container. The pod then responds based on its restart policy. If a configured timeout value is challenging to be met by the current cluster, this would eventually trigger unnecessary kill and reschedule events on the cluster.
      Note Mind, that a slowness on response could be caused either by local cpu slowness or throttling or by any kind of increased latency in the surrounding infrastructure.
